html:
The Kingdom of Burgundy, also called the Kingdom of Arles, covered the Rhône valley, Provence and what is now western Switzerland, with cities such as Arles, Lyon, Geneva and Besançon. On the map for 1000 to 1200 it lies between France and Italy.

It took its name from the Burgundians, a Germanic people who had a kingdom there in the 400s. When the Carolingian Empire broke up, two Burgundian kingdoms formed, and around 933 King Rudolf II joined them.

In 1032 the last king, Rudolf III, died without a son and left the kingdom to the emperor Conrad II. From then on it was one of the three kingdoms of the Holy Roman Empire, but the emperors rarely went there and local counts and bishops ruled. Bit by bit its lands drifted to France, and by the late 1300s the kingdom was little more than a title.

It should not be confused with the Duchy of Burgundy around Dijon, a French fief, or with the Free County of Burgundy.
